cycles.name: Bare Metal
focuses: Effort calibration on the patterns he already owns: three hard axial-free days plus two walking days, and the first real numbers of his training life.
Daily epicondyle isometrics with grip engineered out of the pull volume, scap-first shoulder work below shoulder height, a measured step baseline, and 3-4 kg off.

paragraphs: Welcome in, Amir. You've trained for three years and nobody has ever shown you what your real numbers are, so that's where we start. Five weeks of clean, honest work on machines and supported lifts, where your back is never under a bar and your shoulder never goes overhead.

Three of your five days are lifting. The other two are walking, and they're not filler. The walking is where most of the weight comes off, and your elbow work happens every single day, at home, whether you train or not.
By the end of this block you should be a few kilos lighter, moving more weight than you are now, and your elbow should be quieter than it is today. That's the whole job for month one.
outcomes: Every lift moving up from week 1 to week 5
Elbow pain lower at the desk
Steps logged daily in Proof, then climbing
Weekly weigh-in, same day, same conditions

cycles.name: Rebar
focuses: First true accumulation, with the weekly dose sized off Cycle 1's own logged data rather than the intake claim.
Free-weight upper enters on cleared technique; the elbow moves to heavy slow resistance, and the dated clinician gate falls on this cycle's opening day.

paragraphs: Cycle two is where the volume goes up and free weights start coming in. You'll have earned that by then, because you'll have five weeks of clean numbers behind you and a back that's been quiet under load.
Your elbow work steps up too. Not more of the same, harder.
Right now you're finding out what you can do. Next you find out how much more there is.
teaser.hook: Bare metal first. Then we build on it.

cycles.name: Keystone
focuses: Axial loading earns its way back, gated on two consecutive back-symptom-free cycles plus filmed technique.
Overhead pressing enters only after a fully pain-free cycle below shoulder height. Heaviest upper top sets so far, volume held.

cycles.name: Ballast
focuses: Mandatory back-off: systemic load down about 40%, effort ceilings capped, movement pool refreshed so it reads as a new programme rather than a punishment.
Calories to maintenance, taken before it's needed. The elbow does not deload, it completes its protocol and comes off into ordinary training.

cycles.name: Foundry
focuses: The strength block: lowest reps, highest loads, run at a shallow deficit so the scale keeps moving while the loads climb.
Everything re-tested against week-1 numbers, every standing restriction re-stamped or referred, and the week he can run without a coach installed.

cards.title: Week one is your calibration
cards.body:
The app never tells you what weight to lift. You find it yourself, every time, against the effort number on the card. RPE 8 means you finish the set with about two reps left in you. Not crawling, not easy.

On a movement you've never done, go lighter than you think. Do the first set, see how hard it was, then adjust. Getting it wrong on set one is the point of set one.

  • Week to week: if you hit all the reps and it felt easier than the target, put a little more on next time.
  • If the reps were a grind or you missed some, stay on the same weight and repeat the week.
  • Going lighter is not failing. Bad sleep, long day, something feels off, drop the weight. That's you reading yourself properly.

Two things are lighter on purpose in week one. Do 3 sets on the chest press instead of 4, and do the back extension with no weight at all, arms crossed on your chest. Add from week two.

cards.title: When to stop, and when to see someone
cards.body:
You've got three things we're working around. Your left elbow, your left shoulder, and your lower back. Here's exactly what to do when one of them talks to you.

Normal and fine: muscles burning, being stiff the next day, feeling tired. Keep going. That's training.

  • Mild and fading during the set — finish it, write it in your log.
  • Building through the set, or changing how you move — stop that exercise, use the swap on the card, message me.
  • Sharp, shooting, numb, tingling, or just new and strange — stop the session. Message me before your next one.

And a date for you. Around 21 September I'm reviewing your elbow and shoulder. If they're not measurably better by then, you're going to a physio. Not because anything went wrong, but because six weeks is long enough to find out and I'm not letting this sit for months. Before then, anything that wakes you at night, goes numb, or starts earlier each session, tell me straight away.

cards.title: Telling me it hurts costs you nothing
cards.body:
Most people hide pain from their coach because they think they'll get told to stop training. I want to be clear with you before it ever comes up. Telling me something hurts gets you a change, never a ban.

  • Elbow sore on a pull? Straps go on and we change the handle. You still train your back.
  • Shoulder pinching on a press? We drop the incline or change the machine. You still press.
  • Back tight on the leg press? We change the seat and the depth. You still train legs.
  • Everything sore and you slept four hours? We shorten the session. You still turn up.

The only thing that actually costs you progress is not telling me. If I don't know, I can't change anything, and you end up training around it on your own and making it worse. Say it early and it stays small.

cards.title: Your elbow, and the real reason it hurts
cards.body:
Your elbow isn't sore because of the gym. It's sore because of your desk and your phone. That's roughly fifty hours a week of load on it, against three hours of training. Most of the fix isn't in the gym.

Every day, training or not: rest your forearm on your thigh, palm down, arm straight, and hold a light weight up against gravity. Five holds of 45 seconds, two minutes rest between. Sore arm only.

Pain picks the weight, not effort. It should sit at 3 out of 10 or less while you hold, and be no worse the next morning. If the pain climbs while you're holding, the weight is too heavy. Halve it.

  • Keep your forearm supported on the desk, don't hold it in the air.
  • Bring the mouse in close so your wrist isn't bent back all day.
  • Hold your phone in the other hand, or prop it up.
  • Get off the keyboard for a minute every half hour.
  • Carry your bag and your laptop in the other hand for now.

cards.title: Where the weight actually comes off
cards.body:
Here's the honest version. All three of your lifting sessions put together burn less than adding a few thousand steps a day. Training is what keeps your muscle while you lose fat. The walking and the food are what actually take the weight off.

Week one, don't change anything. Just let Proof count your steps so we see your real number. From week two you get a target built off that, and it climbs.

Same with food. I'm not giving you a meal plan this month. Get protein into every meal and be consistent, and log it in Proof so we can both see it. You told me your eating is up and down. That one thing is worth more than anything I could add to your programme.

cards.title: About those five hours
cards.body:
You rated your sleep 9 out of 10 and then told me you get five to six hours. Those two things don't go together. The quality might be great, there just isn't enough of it.

This matters more than usual right now because you're eating less. When you're short on sleep and in a deficit, more of what you lose comes off your muscle instead of your fat. Same effort, worse result.

I'm not asking you to fix it overnight. Log it in Proof every day so we can put your sleep next to your training and your weight and see it properly. If we get you to seven hours, everything else in this programme works better.

cards.title: Why there is no squat
cards.body:
You told me squats put pressure on your lower back, and you were right to stop doing them. Nothing this month puts a bar on your back or a pad on your shoulders. The leg press and the back extension do the same job with your spine out of it.

That's not forever. A quiet, pain free month is what earns the bar back, and that's month three in your plan. The back extension is the one that gets you there. It teaches your back to hold a strong position instead of just avoiding load.

One rule on it. Stop at a straight line, never past it. If you arch back at the top you're doing the exact thing we're protecting you from.
